content: The pooled estimates derived from the studies do not necessarily represent the outcomes associated with the treatment regimens recommended in the 2011 WHO Guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). This is due to the heterogeneity in study designs, patient populations, and treatment protocols. The shorter MDR-TB regimens dataset is based on recently conducted studies, some of which are ongoing. These studies involved carefully selected patients, and all data were prospectively collected as part of a research protocol. Patients in these studies were uniformly treated with a standardized regimen. In contrast, the longer MDR-TB regimens dataset is derived from older studies, many of which were retrospective in nature and used data collected for clinical purposes rather than research. The majority of patients in the longer regimens group received individualized therapy, with significant variability in the number and type of drugs used, as well as the duration of treatment. The shorter regimens, lasting up to 12 months, were compared to longer regimens, which typically lasted 18 months or more. However, the longer regimens group pooled data from studies with substantial differences in drug combinations, treatment durations, and approaches (standardized versus individualized). As a result, the pooled estimates may not accurately reflect the outcomes of the regimens recommended by the WHO. In the shorter regimen studies, relapse data were only available from the Bangladesh cohort. High-level resistance to gatifloxacin (MIC ≥ 2 mg/mL) was associated with unsuccessful treatment outcomes, while low-level resistance was not. Among patients with ofloxacin-resistant MDR-TB in the shorter regimen group, high-level gatifloxacin resistance was documented in 15 patients, low-level resistance in 13, and gatifloxacin MIC was not measured in 4 patients. The use of later-generation fluoroquinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, or levofloxacin) was compared to the use of ofloxacin or no fluoroquinolone in MDR-TB regimens. Treatment success rates were higher in patients receiving later-generation fluoroquinolones, but the certainty of evidence was low due to methodological limitations, including confounding by indication and selection bias. The use of second-line injectable agents (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin) was also evaluated. Patients receiving these agents as part of MDR-TB regimens had higher treatment success rates compared to those who did not receive them. However, the evidence was limited by the observational nature of the studies, the individualized treatment approaches, and the potential for confounding. In summary, while shorter MDR-TB regimens show promise in terms of efficacy and feasibility, the evidence base is limited by the small number of studies, methodological differences, and potential biases. Further research is needed to confirm the findings and optimize treatment strategies for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
